en.justification: As it was fashionable in the era to invite prominent personalities to perform on stage or to attend as members of the audience, the Marquis Gianfrancesco Aldrovandi Marescotti and his wife Lucrezia were among the actors of the opening performance of this small theatre inside the Aldovrandi villa.
Following the destruction of St. George’s Hall, which was used by the Bavarian court as a theatre, Cuvilliés designed a new opera house.

en.name: Façade, ground-plan and sections of the opera house in Eszterháza
en.artist: Opera design (after fire): Michael Stöger painter/sculptor: Johann Friedrich Schrott
en.justification: Supported by the patronage of Prince Miklós (Nicolaus) II Esterházy, F. J. Haydn served as *Kappelmeister* (Director of music and performance) and court composer at the Esterházy court.

Even though puppet theatres and plays were fashionable during the Baroque-Rococo era, only a few marionettes and dedicated theatres from the period are extant. This precious *teatrino* is a rare and unique example, therefore. The diagonal perspective of the backdrop and wings show the influence of the Bibienas.

Musical life is documented here from the 12th century; it is known that musical theatre was performed in the abbey school from the 17th century, and that throughout the 18th century, the monastery was famous for its talented musicians. This theatre hall was inaugurated in 1725 under the Abbott Rupert Ness. The illusory gallery, which is held up by *trompe l’oeil* columns and opens out into the infinite space of the ceiling fresco, are good examples of illusionistic theatre painting.

en.name: Interior of Teatro dei Vigilanti
en.justification: The theatre-loving members of the Accademia dei Fortunati requested a new theatre for the citizens of Portoferraio in 1814 after their theatre in the Villa Mulino, Elba, had been requisitioned as a residence by Napoleon. In exchange, Napoleon selected for them the 17th-century Chiesa della Carmine, which the architect Paolo Bargigli then re-designed as a theatre.

en.name: The stage curtain of the Teatro dei Vigilanti
en.justification: The original Napoleonic stage-curtain, painted by Vincenzo Antonio Revelli, an artist of Napoleonic court, is still in use today following painstaking restoration. Its bucolic image represents Napoleon sitting in an idyllic landscape among shepherds and animals.
The print documents the theatricality, splendour and excessiveness of a banquet.

Since according to Hungarian law the country belongs to the Holy Crown, which is seen as the body of the country, it is tempting to state that this procession is like the triumphal entry of the king to his capital city.

This fictitious triumphal entry of the victorious hero echoes the most pompous triumphs of Roman military leaders and emperors. Similar to the triumphal entries of antiquity, the procession is approaching a magnificent triumphal arch; an indispensable attribute of a *trionfo*.
The manuscript commemorates a special type of festivity, a poetry competition.

The joyous event of the *Festa della porchetta* (Pork Feast) was one of Bologna’s most important festivities to entertain the citizens of the city, but with political undertones. Besides roasting and distribution of the pork, various practical jokes, plays and theatrical performances were organised.

This splendid piece recalls the joyful feasts of the aristocracy and the gallantries of the Rococo era. As was commonly seen at balls during the era, the musicians are separated in a *loggia* in the background.
In the foreground a pair of *commedia dell'arte* figures is seen playing music, drinking, dancing and mocking.

Via del Corso was dreamed up by Pope Paul II as a route for festive events and *palii*, horse races. At the end of this major thoroughfare, the churches appear like a grandiose *frons* *scaneae* or a monumental proscenium arch, behind which opens up the great stage of the Piazza del Popolo. The magnificent square has hosted many solemn entries of popes and royal guests (Bernini created an ephemeral triumphal arch with inscriptions for the solemn entry (*ingresso*) of Christina of Sweden in 1655, commissioned by Pope Alexander VII). Carnivals have taken place at the site, and Napoleon's army even processed on floats towards via del Corso.

Bernini's Fountain of the Rivers, positioned on a site known for the martyrdom of Christians in Antique Rome, is a symbol of the triumph of the Church and of innocence. Such permanent structures were often informed by the opportunities for experimentation that the design of ephemeral structures for festivals offered.

Bernini's Fountain of the Rivers, positioned on a site known for the martyrdom of Christians in Antique Rome, is a symbol of the triumph of the Church and of innocence. Such permanent structures were often informed by the opportunities for experimentation that the design of ephemeral structures for festivals offered.

Bernini's Fountain of the Rivers, positioned on a site known for the martyrdom of Christians in Antique Rome, is a symbol of the triumph of the Church and of innocence. Such permanent structures were often informed by the opportunities for experimentation that the design of ephemeral structures for festivals offered.

Bernini's Fountain of the Rivers, positioned on a site known for the martyrdom of Christians in Antique Rome, is a symbol of the triumph of the Church and of innocence. Such permanent structures were often informed by the opportunities for experimentation that the design of ephemeral structures for festivals offered.

The Piazza Navona was the setting of magnificent festivities enriched by fireworks displays and for which the apparati were constructed. The festivities included trionfi, giostre, tornei, caroselli; festivities of other nations (Spanish, French and German; to celebrate military victories or dynastic events), religious processions; carnivals, masquerades, theatrical performances.

This splendid, picturesque and solemn urban site was a popular venue for many different types of festivities. For festive events the façade of the Trinitá dei Monti, the steps and the square below would be embellished with decorations. The *apparati* would be placed on the steps, in the square or in front of the church.

en.detail_name: The low entry-wing of the Jesuit college with the square in front
en.justification: The low entry-wing of the Jesuit college was constructed to form a *frons scaneae* (monumental backdrop) to the theatrical stage of the square below.

Echoing the Spanish Steps in Rome, the Baroque staircase of the Jesuit complex is an impressive, angular construction with powerful but harmonious convex and concave angles and views. It is one of the most dynamic structures in Croatia’s urban landscape.
The nave of the church opens up to the sanctuary, where sections in the wall are presented like miniature theatrical stages.
The ceiling painting opens up to the heavens, where in what appears to be an eternal theatrical stage, the glorious figure of St. Ignatius kneels.

This imposing site was a popular venue for festivals, set against the backdrop of the Castel St. Angelo (site of the *Girandola* a special fireworks display), during the Baroque era. The bridge (a route for pilgrims to the Vatican) was a pilgrimage site, a special monument to the Golgota and resemblant of a *Via Crucis* (Stations of the Cross), because of the statues relating to Christ’s Passion. While crossing the bridge, therefore, the faithful could meditate upon Christ’s passion. It was during this “trespass” that the pilgrim’s compassion transported him from the role of spectator to a participant in Christ’s Passion.

Expressions and tools borrowed from the theatre helped to create this special site of devotion. To approach the church, pilgrims were obliged to pass through an impressive *Via Crucis*, during which they could reflect on the life, the Passion of Christ and the Redemption. On their way, their compassion would make them feel part of the Passion, experiencing katharsis, similar to watching a tragedy at the theatre. It should be noted that the stage-set according to this particular genre is the human soul itself, whereby the stairway is an allegory for mankind's rise from earthly desires and sins to redemption through Christ.

The water coming from the five holy wounds of Christ symbolises the blood which He shed for mankind. Thus, drinking from this water symbolises the drinking from the water of life and the Holy Communion, and reminds the faithful that the blood of Christ is the water of life for all mankind.

en.detail_name: Interior of the Chapel of the Falls
en.justification: The chapel decoration evokes the landscape of Jerusalem like a theatrical backdrop, with life-size figures in frozen theatrical scenes (as in a panoptic), revealing to the pilgrims the darkest moments of Christ’s Passion.
The final chapel on the ascent is dedicated to the Crucifixion.

en.name: The main altar, general view
en.artist: Design and models of the figures: Manuel Joaquim Álvares de Sousa; figures executed by João Monteiro da Rocha; canopy designed by Carlos Amarante and executed by Master Woodcarver José Francisco Moreira Torres
en.justification: The main altar of the church portrays the strong theatrical effects of light, scenery and perspective.

en.name: The main altar, general view
en.artist: Design and models of the figures: Manuel Joaquim Álvares de Sousa; figures executed by João Monteiro da Rocha; canopy designed by Carlos Amarante and executed by Master Woodcarver José Francisco Moreira Torres
en.justification: Detail of the main altar.

Entering the octagonal sacristy is like standing on the stage in a theatre. Surrounded by heavy gilt, the glittering auditorium shimmers in the diffused light of the ceiling lantern. The real performers are the 89 reliquary sculptures that are placed in the niches all around. The reality of space and time merges into the sacred and eternal timelessness of the saints who are illuminated by the theatrical light of the ceiling lantern and bathed in the reflection of gilt.
Detail of the wall niches and statues of the sanctuary.

The altarpiece is similar to a *sacra rappresentazione*, a Passion Play, or an ephemeral decoration for a religious festival in a church. The Agony of St. Bernard, played out as if it were a real-time-and-space scene, leads to the eternal and sacred space ruled by the Virgin Mary. The musical instruments held by the angels are representations of contemporary instruments with which viewers would have been familiar at banquets, concerts or operas. The rows of cherubs and angels are formed in the shape of a bow around the monumental proscenium arch.

This magnificent church interior is a breathtaking example of Baroque pomp, illusion and theatricality. The mastery of architectural illusion produces a space that appears to be longer than it really is.

The high altar appears like a scene from a theatrical performance, behind a proscenium, which connects the real world of the church with the biblical, heavenly, eternal world represented by the Holy Trinity. The gestures and postures of the Four Fathers of the Church evoke those used by actors who were popular in Baroque theatres and in the *sacre rappresentazioni*, the Passion plays. What makes this altarpiece unique is that the the wings – the "scenery" – are interchangeable just as scenes are changed during a theatrical performance.
The scene opens the space upwards, merging together historical scenes relating to the history of the church building and images of heaven.
With the usage of perspective solutions, light-effects and strong contrast between the black and the richly gilt surfaces, this theatrical space is a perfect site for *sacre rappresentazioni*.

Above the high altar, a scene reminiscent of theatre shows the Triumphal Christ between side-wings that have been shortened using perspective. The light, reflecting off the gilt and illuminating the scene, enhances the viewer’s illusion of peering into heavenly Jerusalem.

The altar space, constructed entirely within the theatrical conception of representation, accommodates figures and architectural motifs that are set back, thus allowing the viewer to enter the space of the protagonists, and thereby allowing them to absorb and enter the space.
The kings with their theatrical gestures are represented both as spectators and participants – who like the viewer – stand on the border between the real world and heavenly Jerusalem.
Some of the figures are represented with emphasis on theatrical gesture.
Angels, like heavenly narrators, invite us to view the scene.

en.name: The Birth of the Virgin Mary Altar (high altar)
en.location: Choir, Parish Church Birth of the Virgin Mary, St. Peter and Paul, former Convent Church of Augustine Canons
en.justification: Like a scene from *theatrum sacrum* which has been paused temporarily, the high altar opens out in front of the viewer, bathed in daylight. The saturation of the light is perfect: in the background the natural colouration of the marble columns and the architraves are enlivened by the white marble bodies, gilt draperies and ornaments of the protagonists. As in the theatre, composition, gesture, posture and light are employed to maximum affect to create drama and pathos.

In this amazing horseshoe-shaped auditorium, the splendid princely box that served the Bavarian prince electors is embraced by 24 balconies in four rows. The audience is seated according to social status and rank: in the ground-floor boxes is the city nobility; on the first floor the court aristocracy; on the second floor the lower-ranking noblemen; and in the third circle, at the top, are the court officials.
A small rectangular hall with two rows of boxes comprised the seating arrangement in this theatre, which was part of a family residence.

This elaborate model in wood faithfully shows the original architectural and decorative structure by Bibiena: a huge auditorium with four rows of boxes, a gallery above them, the orchestra seat, the *frons scenae* (the back of the stage) and a section of the stage.
This perspective scene represents the virtuosity and revolutionary *prospettiva per angolo* (diagonal perspective) of Francesco Galli Bibiena.
The elaborate skill of perspective is seen in this masterpiece by one of Europe’s most genuine and skilful theatrical artists of his time, Ferdinando Galli Bibiena.
Plays written by some of Europe’s most famous playwrights, and also sometimes by the owner of the villa, were played on the stage of this villa-theatre.
Ceremonial coaches, such as this magnificent, richly carved and gilded royal coach, were used in the arrival to and departure from festive events and in ceremonial processions.

Another very important aspect of festivities was water. Spectacular feasts were organised at which floating vessels or ships on rivers or lakes (sometimes artificial) were central, and sometimes included *naumachia* (water battle). Magnificent vessels were built to transport royals and aristocrats to the site of the feast.

Venetian mirrors not only increased the pomp of the gilt environment, but also visually increased the space inside the cabin. Representations of a river and the sea within the landscape bring to the cabin-environment the all-important element of water.
Gilt lamps made evening events even more magical.
A coronation was a most important ceremonial occasion.

Costumes, textiles, colour and jewellery played an important role in festivities. This magnificent late 17th-century gown illustrates the luxurious sartorial fashions of the aristocracy: the colourful and fine textiles, lacework and embroidery, the fashionable design and elegant accessories. The aristocracy had a particular admiration for precious stones, especially pearls, which are worn by the subject of the painting illustrated here.

The impressive representation of the family’s ancestors wearing ceremonial clothes reveals the social status, rank or military career of the individuals. The cut and pattern of the women’s clothes follow the latest sartorial fashions.

This formal portrait provides a unique opportunity to admire and study the elegant clothes, not only of a Bolognese noble family, but also the clothing worn by men and women of different generations as well.

This sumptuously decorated great hall was further elaborated for ceremonies and banquets. Meditating on the acts of St. Bernard represented on the walls, the guests were incorporated into the time and space of the saint while also participating in the festivities in the present. The theatre of illusory paintings imitating stucco decorations, statues and small trees in buckets, would have been the subject of further marvel for the guests.

The musicians’ gallery was placed at the level of the “open” ceiling of the hall. Thus, on one hand, the musicians were entirely separated from the high-ranking guests, while on the other, music (essential for creating a festive atmosphere) appeared to come from “nowhere”, from the open sky, like the music of the spheres. The ceiling above the gallery is painted with an illusory fresco evoking infinity.

In front of the massive Corinthian columns which run the length of the walls in this magnificent Ceremonial hall are powerful, life-size figures of emperors. Each with his own posture and gesture, the figures interact, with each other, the space of the hall, and the guests.

en.detail_name: Ceiling fresco in the Imperial Hall
en.justification: The illusory ceiling fresco opens up the space of the hall, lifting up the viewer from an earthly assembly into a heavenly one, and ascending the eternal view to the sacred realm.

Guests at festive events were amazed by Francesco Galli Bibiena’s skilful illusory wall paintings using *prospettiva all’angolo* (corner perspective), which was invented by the Bibienas, and employed on theatrical stages throughout Europe.
The painted illusory architecture amalgamates with the real architecture below the ceiling.

Exceptionally skilfully, Bibiena’s perspective reveals multiple levels of illusion to the viewer. In the foreground, the painted figure of Hercules imitates a marble statue standing on an illusory stone balcony. The viewer’s eye is then guided to the sumptuous gallery, where a half-pulled red curtain opens up to a view of fresh, green vegetation in a garden behind it. The curtain-pull, a visual pun, is placed with its tassel dangling on the painted balustrade, further developing the illusory effect.
Everywhere by way of opened doors, windows and a lantern, this magnificent ballroom is bathed in light. The theatrical effect of the light is increased by the fact that the room is white.
Magnificent white-stucco trophies decorate each corner of the ballroom ceiling.
A magnificent site of festive events.

en.name: Ballroom (Ceremonial hall, Festsaal)
en.artist: Design and ceiling frescos: Gregorio Guglielmi (1714–1773); stucco: Franz-Xaver Feichtmayr (1735–1803), Simpert Feichtmayr (1732–1806); carving: Placidus Verhelst (1727–1778)
en.justification: The spectacular ballroom is a fine example of a private Rococo banqueting or ceremonial hall. A site of social gatherings, balls, receptions and other festive gatherings, its longitudinal walls are punctuated with windows that in daytime bathe the room in shimmery light. In the evening, the glittering lights of the crystal chandeliers would have reflected in the richly gilded mirrors placed in between the windows, thus achieving an equally magical effect in the room at night as by day.

A fascinating example of *maison de plaisance* in what is known as the *Lustschlösser* genre, a special type of castle or palace in the Bavarian countryside, which were built especially for festive events, hunting, small social gatherings and banquets, musical entertainment or as small private retreats.

en.name: Spiegelsaal (Central ceremonial hall)
en.artist: Designed by François Cuvilliés (1695–1768); stucco: Johann Baptist Zimmermann (1680–1758); carving: Johann Joachim Dietrich (1690–1753)
en.justification: Mirrors have the ability to open up and multiply space, thus, stepping into this hall with its silver decoration representing nature, one feels transported into the enchanted lands of Arcadia.

However eternally frozen in marble, the Barberinis seem to be peering out from their balconies through the visitors entering the church, turning towards the altarpiece and pointing both to the altar and towards the church. The curtain that seems to be a real velvet woven through with gold threads feels like just pulled away right now.
The fresco combines all the scenic elements of architectural *quadratura*: light and shade, perspective, group and scenic composition, to maximise its theatrical impact.
The chancel arch, like the proscenium arch surrounding a stage, reveals the stage-like scene of the illusory altarpiece.

The illusory painting behind the main altar appears as if it were a scene from a play. The device, known as *theatrum sacrum* or *sacra rappresentazione*, brings this pictorial representation from the Life of Christ into the viewer’s present. In this theatre, the faithful, in some mysterious, secret and miraculous way are crossing the border between the temporary world and the eternal world.
The magnificent illusory painting of a cupola has hidden spiritual and symbolic meanings.

The illusory façade paintings appear as if they are scenes from a play showing at an outdoor theatre, or perhaps, actual scenes from the Bible. In Oberammergau, *theatrum sacrum* or Passion Plays are still performed today just as they have been since 1634.
With its shining gilt, the *Resurrection* represents the transformation to the eternal and the heavenly.
View of *Lüftmalerei* (lit. “air paintings”), which are a form of Bavarian *trompe l’oeil* or illusory painting.
The use of natural light and the reflective nature of the silver and the gold accentuate the theatrical effects of the altar.

en.detail_name: The Miraculous Picture of the Virgin Mary
en.justification: A splendid theatrical set-up where the painting of the Virgin Mary is akin to setting a stage within the middle of another stage.

The altar-frame, which acts much like the proscenium arch surrounding a theatrical stage or the set built around a *sacra rappresentazione*, even one built temporarily on a city square, makes this scene from the Conversion of St. Paul appear as if it were being performed on stage. The gestures would have been familiar to contemporary audiences as they were translated to fine art from the theatre.
Detail of the saint on the left.
Detail of the saint on the right.
Farinelli was Europe’s most influential and celebrated soprano castrato of the Baroque opera stage.
Naples-born Domenico Scarlatti reformed the music scene in Portugal by introducing Italian opera. His new musical dramaturgy, scores and artistic innovations also influenced the Berlin opera.
The puppet, dressed as Hamlet, still wears its original clothes.

This is the type of theatre where actors’ roles were replaced by one of the most important elements of the festivities, water. Based on the high-level technical skills of engineers, mechanics and scenographers, water played the starring role in a spectacle of watery “sunbeams”, which sprang up and then cascaded, to mellifluous or thunderous sound effects.

en.detail_name: Aerial view: to the right part of the water theatre can be seen
en.justification: Beside the spectacular effects of water springing up and cascading in fountains and niches (some of them giving the illusion of being natural), this special type of water theatre included fascinating performances by automatons, some of which danced or played instruments pumped and moved by air and water. It all seemed so natural, but behind their performances were a highly skilled workforce of hydraulic engineers, architects, mechanics and musicians. These kinetic figures, and the hydro-engineering systems behind them, were the beloved, highly expensive toys of princes from the 16th to the 18th century.
One of the theatrical niches.

en.detail_name: Cascade with artificial rocks, niches and a pond
en.justification: The spectacle and sound of water together made for an impressive performance.
Arriving through an aqueduct, the water flowed in channels and streams all around, making for a picturesque scene in the *nympheaum*.

Palazzo Barberini was built on and incorporated into the site of the antique theatre temple, the Sanctuary of Fortuna Primigenia. The seating capacity of this spectacular, well-preserved, semi-circular auditorium was around 500 people. Situated at the back of the auditorium is the *porticus in summa cavea* (a gallery at the top of a cave), with two rows of columns at the top and a circular-form temple erected behind it, crowning the slope. The rows of seating are not original.
The 15th-century well in front of the palace façade was built on top of the small orchestra pit of the former Roman theatre.

Because of the short depth of space between the end of the auditorium and orchestra areas, some scholars hold that there was no permanent stage in the theatre but only an ephemeral, wooden structure to accommodate all types of performances. Others suppose that the breathtaking countryside was the backdrop and scenery for performances. In front of the temple-theatre complex, on the lower level, stands a Corinthian-order triple *porticus*.
Detail of the façade of the palace, the auditorium and the well.
An archway erected to honour Admiral Leonardo Foscolo is also the actual entry to the city of Dubrovnik.
Echoing Roman triumphal arches, this arch probably was once decorated with a statue of Admiral Foscolo in whose honour it was erected.
The cartouche holds a commemorative inscription dedicated to Admiral Foscolo.

Although Maria Theresia did not make a triumphal entry into Vác when she visited the city in 1764, this triumphal arch commemorates her visit, which was celebrated with other festive events such as illuminations as well.

en.detail_name: Attic, south side of the arch
en.justification: Inscription and *tondos* (circular engravings in high-relief) on the south-side attic of the arch.

en.detail_name: Attic, north side of the arch
en.justification: Inscription and *tondos* (circular engravings in high-relief) on the north-side attic of the arch.

This is an excellent example of how decorative features or *apparato* (temporary structures) from festive occasions influenced permanent monuments. Creating the illusion of a triumphal arch, this splendid fountain acts as a triumphal receptacle for the water that arrives in Rome to serve the city.
The castle was commissioned as a festive site by Elector Max Emanuel II, who gave it to his wife, Maria Antonia, as a wedding gift to commemorate their marriage.
The site of splendid banquets, the illusory ceiling fresco opens the space upwards.
The site of splendid balls, receptions and other ceremonies.
Gardens were popular sites for festive events.
A site of magnificent festive events, which almost like a monumental picture book, commemorates these events in frescoes around the walls.
The frescoes commemorate significant events in Bologna’s history.
A detailed depiction of one of the most splendid events in the history of Bologna. The scene appears as if it were a theatrical production within a proscenium arch.
The scene of the papal blessing of 1095 is represented as if it were a monumental scene in a play. The costumes and the scenographic solutions are rooted in the theatre designs of the Bibienas.
The site of magnificent royal ceremonies.

In this festive-theatrical representation, the allegorical figures pertaining to the virtues of a good reign are represented as if they were characters making a triumphal entry (*trionfo*) on an eternal stage.

A *sacro monte* connecting the secular and sacred, beginning in the Garden of the Kings and terminating with the dominant Sanctuary of Our Lady of Good Remedy. The theatricality is sensed in the fantastic view of the stairs, the *azulejos*, vegetation, fountains and noise of water all around. To trace the roots of this venue one might look to the Villa d'Este in Tivoli and in the Garden of the Bom Jesus.
Resembling a scenic urban square with an obelisk.
The façade of the church limits the view upwards, like a theatrical backdrop.
The pilgrim’s experience of this theatrically-formulated site was not simply that of a spectator, but as an active participant in the holy events.
A site of summer social gatherings and relaxation, the amazing *trompe l’oeil* paintings are rooted in the scenic tradition and create an illusion of standing in the middle of a glorious garden.

The walls and doors are covered with *trompe l’oeil* vegetation to the extent that one is close to losing all sense of orientation; almost convinced that one can hear gurgling water and nearly intoxicated by the overpowering smell of the flowers. We are in a garden-paradise; an imaginary Arcadia; in the territory of love.
The illusory paintings of stone vases that appear to be stage props cheat the eyes even more with the painted flowers in them.

en.detail_name: Flora and her companion on the ceiling
en.justification: Flora, with her companion, appears in the sky of Arcadia.

The magnificent ceremonial staircase is painted with high-quality *quadratura* and *trompe l'oeil* paintings. The scenes on the side-walls are like small theatrical stages; behind the curtains we glimpse splendid painted halls with rows of vaults and columns, like looking through a sketchbook of set-designs belonging to a scenographer. The architectural *quadratura* of the ceiling elongates the space upwards, creating the fake illusion of balconies, halls and stuccoes, until reaching the sky and an illusion of infinity.
Stepping into the bedroom the splendid stuccowork opens up, surprisingly, like monumental scenery, to the nuptial bed.

For Prince Miklós (Nikolaus) II Esterházy this magnificent ceremonial hall was one of the main sites for indoor festivities, where in 1773, Queen Maria Theresia joined him in the festivities for two days.
One side of the Ceremonial Hall adjoins Haydn Hall, the site of festivities and Haydn’s music, while on the other side, is the *cour d’honneur*.
A splendid site for social gatherings during the summer months.

en.detail_name: Aereal view showing the cour d’honneur and parts of the formal garden
en.justification: As the site of social gatherings, fireworks displays, illuminations, theatrical plays and other princely entertainments, the garden played an extremely important role in the festive calendar at Esterházy palace in Eszterháza. The *cour d’honneur* was used for festive parades.

en.name: Festive sites in the Queluz Royal Palace, Theatre hall
en.justification: This amazing summer palace contained a small theatre.
The site of magnificent receptions, audiences or other royal ceremonies.
This splendid garden also hosted elaborate festive events.
Representative staircases also hosted royal festivities in Queluz.

Delighting in music and theatrical performances, Count Questenberg created a hall-theatre in the east wing of the castle. Antonio and Giuseppe Galli Bibiena were employed by the count as stage- and set-designers and the pair also invented stage machinery, working alongside local artists who were employed to paint the props they designed.
An 18th-century drawing representing the monumental complex of Jaroměřice nad Rokytnou chateau.
The garden was a favourite site for festivities.
Representing the elaborate *apparato* (firework machine) and the pyrotechnical affects it produced, this print commemorates a festive event of the past.
The final highlight of the feast was the cannon-fire. From the explosion a two-headed imperial eagle rose, and then from the mighty flames an inscription emerged.

en.detail_name: The representation of the Virgin Mary
en.justification: The coronation of the Virgin Mary represents the idea of the Holy Virgin as the Queen of Moravia and the patron saint of the country.
Miraculous images, signs and props like this sumptuous silver processional altar, were carried in religious processions.
The back of the altarpiece.

This etching is a fine document preserved from the solemn, dramatic and touching ephemeral decorations (*apparati*) which were made in Bologna during Holy Week in the 18th century. The illusory painted decoration, the strong perspective scenery and effects of light and shade are all tools of theatrical illusion.

The sculpted and pictorial decorations of a *castrum doloris* commemorate the important events of the life of the deceased, praising his faith, or glory, as if it were a theatrical production. The decoration of Auersperg’s catafalque includes military trophies commemorating his career and victories. Just as if the scene were from a play, and already in a sacred, eternal space and time, the figures representing Auersperg’s ancestors are making solemn testimonies to the deceased using the language of theatrical gesture, spinning around the coffin under the vault in the middle like mute performers surrounding the protagonist in this *teatro alla morte*.

A piece used in one of the most theatrically staggering and dignified religious festivities: the ceremony of the Adoration of Corpus Christi. The theatrical effect of this magnificent piece would have been raised still further by its presentation.

*Auto de Fé* was the ritual of public penance declared by the Spanish or Portuguese inquisition on condemned heretics and apostates. It was considered as theatrical ritual in the Baroque era, which in modern times seems bizarre.
This print commemorates the event as a memory and also as a dramatic reminder to those considered as heretics by the Catholic Church.

en.name: Magnificent *apparato* in a form of a triumphal arch. Silver Altar and Coronation Set.
